address_historical: Blue Island Avenue at Throop Street over railroad tracks
owner_or_developer: City of Chicago and affected railroads
postfire_code_context: Iron and masonry infrastructure was consistent with post-fire preferences for durable construction, although grade separation was its primary purpose.
notes: Begun October 15, 1875 and completed August 25, 1876. Andreas reports a total cost of $102,173.99.

address_historical: Milwaukee Avenue over the Chicago & North Western, Chicago Milwaukee & St. Paul, and Pittsburgh Chicago & St. Louis railroad tracks
architect_or_builder: American Bridge Company (south portion); Leighton Bridge Company (north portion)
owner_or_developer: City of Chicago and affected railroads
structural_system: iron bridge superstructure; substructure not stated
postfire_code_context: Large iron infrastructure reflected the post-fire shift toward durable, noncombustible public works.
notes: Opened May 25, 1876. Andreas called it the city's largest and most expensive viaduct and reported a cost of $140,371.55; the construction start was not located.

demolition_cause: destroyed by the gale of May 5, 1876
address_historical: Fuller Street crossing of the Chicago River
postfire_code_context: The destroyed wooden bridge predated the 1874 citywide prohibition on new wood construction.
notes: The $7,500 wooden bridge erected in 1865 was destroyed on May 5, 1876. This is a physical-loss event, not 1876 construction.

canonical_name: West Division Pumping Works extension project
address_historical: West Division waterworks site
postfire_code_context: Water-supply expansion was a post-fire resilience investment; precise ordinance and fireproofing requirements require engineering-record review.
notes: Andreas says the extension was projected in 1876 and entered regular service in July 1884. Reported machinery cost was $257,500 and total project cost $371,681.01. No 1876 completion is claimed.

canonical_name: Cook County Hospital clinical amphitheater and corridors
address_historical: Between Wood and Lincoln Streets and Harrison and Polk Streets
address_modern: Cook County Health campus near 1835 W Harrison St
original_use: clinical teaching amphitheater and pavilion connections
structural_system: red brick with stone trim; 600-seat amphitheater
postfire_code_context: Masonry institutional additions reflected post-fire concern for separation and fire resistance, outside the 1871 burned district.
notes: The clinical amphitheater and connecting corridors were built during 1876-77. The 600-seat amphitheater is retained as a distinct phase, not counted as a 1876 completion.

alternate_names: St. Patrick's girls' school; St. Patrick's female school
address_historical: Adams Street immediately west of St. Patrick's Church
owner_or_developer: St. Patrick's Catholic parish; Sisters of Charity of St. Vincent de Paul
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Frame school immediately west of St. Patrick's Church
postfire_code_context: Brick construction conformed to the post-1874 citywide prohibition on new wood buildings.
notes: A large twelve-room brick school was erected in 1876 at a reported cost of about $24,000 and accommodated roughly 500 pupils. Andreas uses both academy and school language.

address_historical: St. Michael's parish property near North Avenue and New Church Street
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Clergy house damaged in the Great Chicago Fire
postfire_code_context: The work restored fire-damaged institutional fabric rather than creating a wholly new building.
notes: Partly restored in 1872, the clergy house was completed in 1876. The current building's degree of surviving 1876 fabric requires architectural survey.

address_historical: Northeast corner of Market and Hill Streets
postfire_code_context: Brick construction complied with the post-1874 citywide restriction on new wood buildings.
notes: Cornerstone laid in October 1876; the approximately $40,000 church was dedicated October 6, 1878. Included for its exact start event, not as a 1876 completion.

alternate_names: St. Joseph's Home for the Friendless; industrial school and refuge
address_historical: Corner of May and Eleventh Streets
original_use: industrial school and refuge for homeless girls
postfire_code_context: A charitable-institution project after the fire; material and code compliance require permit or diocesan confirmation.
notes: The home was commenced in 1876 and later enlarged and completed in 1885 at a reported cost of $16,000. Its first usable phase and opening year remain unresolved.

address_historical: Northeast corner of West Adams and Throop Streets
postfire_code_context: Brick construction complied with the post-1874 citywide restriction on new wood buildings.
notes: Construction began in summer 1876. The more-than-$45,000 church, seating about 800, was dedicated January 6, 1877.

address_historical: Dearborn and Delaware Streets
structural_system: masonry church; exact materials not stated
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: New England Congregational Church damaged or destroyed in the Great Chicago Fire
postfire_code_context: Permanent reconstruction occurred within the North Side fire-limits environment.
notes: Rebuilding commenced in 1874 and was completed January 1, 1876; the rebuilt church was dedicated January 2. Library finding aids independently confirm the intersection and identify an exterior photograph.

address_historical: Southeast corner of Lincoln and Jackson Streets
postfire_code_context: Brick construction complied with the post-1874 citywide restriction on new wood buildings.
notes: The $8,000 brick church was dedicated on the first Sunday of January 1876. Construction began after the society organized in 1875.

address_historical: Southwest corner of Indiana Avenue and Twenty-first Street
structural_system: substantial stone masonry; Early French Gothic and Oriental design
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Sinai synagogue at Plymouth Court and Van Buren Street destroyed in 1871
postfire_code_context: A substantial noncombustible temple replaced the congregation's fire-destroyed downtown synagogue.
notes: Commenced about April 1875 and dedicated April 8, 1876. Andreas reports approximately $90,000 including sidewalk, furnishings and organ.

address_historical: Cass Street at Huron Street
owner_or_developer: St. James's Episcopal parish; memorial to James Carter
structural_system: nine bells installed in existing masonry tower
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: St. James's Episcopal Church reconstruction completed in 1875
postfire_code_context: Installed in an already reconstructed masonry church; the event did not enlarge the building shell.
notes: A nine-bell chime was first rung on Christmas Day 1876 as a memorial to James Carter. Bell survival and later replacements require parish-archive review.

canonical_name: St. Paul's Catholic Church first frame building remodel
address_historical: Near Ambrose and Hoyne Streets
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Pre-existing frame building purchased by the parish
postfire_code_context: The parish reused an existing frame structure after the 1874 ban on new wood construction; whether alteration permits treated it as an exception needs confirmation.
notes: The parish organized in 1876, purchased and remodeled a modest frame building near Ambrose and Hoyne, and established a school. A later brick basement is not assigned to 1876.

canonical_name: St. John's Catholic Church bell installation
address_historical: St. John's Catholic Church property
structural_system: bell installed in existing church tower
postfire_code_context: An equipment installation within an existing church; no new combustible building fabric is documented.
notes: The approximately 6,000-pound bell was installed and blessed in 1876 and first rung on St. Patrick's Day. Andreas places construction of a new church in 1877, not 1876.

address_historical: Originally at Thirty-sixth Street and Western Avenue
owner_or_developer: DuPont explosives company; built for Junot Whitehouse
postfire_code_context: Brick construction reflected the post-1874 citywide fire limits; the explosives-company association adds industrial-safety context.
notes: Built in 1875-76 for superintendent Junot Whitehouse and moved one block in 1920. Completion is assigned to the range endpoint rather than an exact completion date.

canonical_name: George M. Pullman Residence initial construction
demolition_cause: demolished after Prairie Avenue's residential decline
address_historical: 1729 South Prairie Avenue
architect_or_builder: Henry S. Jaffray and/or John Mathew Dunphy; later additions by Solon S. Beman
postfire_code_context: Substantial stone construction reflected elite post-fire rebuilding and noncombustible urban construction.
notes: University of Minnesota chronology gives 1876 completion; the Art Institute finding aid indexes competing 1876 design attributions and later 1880s Beman additions. Reported value ranges from $350,000 to $500,000.

address_historical: Dearborn Street
postfire_code_context: Stone residential construction followed Near North Side rebuilding and fire-limit requirements.
notes: National Register documentation gives 1875-76. Evidence of an August 1875 social event at the house indicates occupancy may predate 1876, so the endpoint is retained as a possible completion phase rather than a certain opening.

address_historical: 43-45 Monroe Street; north side of Monroe between State and Wabash
address_modern: 12-14 E Monroe St (historic-numbering crosswalk needs confirmation)
owner_or_developer: Chicago Club; N. K. Fairbank associated with development
structural_system: Baltimore pressed brick with limestone and Berea sandstone; modern Gothic
postfire_code_context: The masonry clubhouse was built inside the post-fire central business district under strengthened fire-limit rules.
notes: Plans were published October 2, 1875 and the building was erected in 1876 on a 50-by-100-foot lot opposite the Palmer House. The secondary chronology gives a 1939 demolition.

address_historical: South side of Monroe Street, center block between Franklin and Market Streets
owner_or_developer: Business sponsors associated with Dwight L. Moody; site associated with John V. Farwell
postfire_code_context: A brick shell inside the central fire limits provided noncombustible enclosure despite the intentionally temporary roof and use.
notes: Erected in 1876 with seating for about 8,000. In 1877 the temporary roof was removed and three stories were added to create six stores, making the tabernacle a documented short-lived phase.

canonical_name: Bemis and McAvoy brewery 1876 ice house
address_historical: West side of South Park Avenue near Twenty-third Street
structural_system: industrial cold-storage structure; exact material not stated
postfire_code_context: Industrial construction followed the citywide 1874 fire-limit extension, but material and permit compliance remain unverified.
notes: One of four spacious ice houses explicitly dated 1872, 1874, 1875 and 1876. The sequence supports a discrete 1876 addition but not a street number or individual-house dimensions.

alternate_names: Michael Brand's brewery; later United States Brewing Company Brand branch
address_historical: Elston Road near Fullerton Avenue
structural_system: substantial brick industrial buildings with machinery
postfire_code_context: Brick industrial construction reflected the post-1874 citywide fire limits, although the complex was itself destroyed by fire in 1885.
notes: The substantial brick brewery and machinery complex was built during 1876-77 for about $300,000; Brand moved the business there in 1877. It burned May 13, 1885.

alternate_names: Clifton House site building; Chicago Public Library quarters
address_historical: Southeast corner of Wabash Avenue and Madison Street
original_use: hotel in upper three stories; stores and offices below
structural_system: existing commercial masonry building; upper three stories converted
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: Commercial and library building erected on the old Clifton House site
postfire_code_context: Conversion of an existing central-business-district masonry building occurred under post-fire occupancy and egress rules; exact permit record is unlocated.
notes: After the Chicago Public Library left in 1876, the upper three stories were converted to the Sands House. Andreas gives a 100-by-132-foot footprint, 120 guest rooms and capacity of about 300.

canonical_name: Anna House opening as New Delavan House
alternate_names: New Delavan House; later Anna House
address_historical: 102 North Clark Street
original_use: hotel in upper four stories above commercial space
postfire_code_context: No 1876 physical construction is documented; the row is retained only as a building-use event.
notes: Opened to the public in 1876 as the New Delavan House. Andreas describes a 100-by-150-foot building, four hotel stories, about 50 rooms and capacity of 100; construction date remains unknown.

canonical_name: Lincoln Park Floating Hospital pier and shelter use
address_historical: Lincoln Park lakefront north of North Avenue
original_use: summer hospital and convalescent care for children
owner_or_developer: Floating Hospital Association; Lincoln Park Commissioners
structural_system: wooden pier with shelter house, railings, hammocks and cots
postfire_code_context: The wooden waterfront installation had a specialized park and pier use; ordinary city building-code applicability is uncertain.
notes: The Association received use of the roughly 400-foot pier in 1876 for a floating-hospital program. Andreas describes a shelter house and care equipment, but does not unambiguously date the shelter's erection; no construction completion is claimed.

canonical_name: Carson, Pirie & Company North Division store opening
alternate_names: Carson Pirie North Side dry-goods house
address_historical: 166-170 North Clark Street
structural_system: existing commercial building; material not stated
postfire_code_context: No physical construction is documented; this is a commercial occupancy event within the post-fire North Division.
notes: Andreas states that Carson, Pirie & Company opened a large dry-goods house at 166-170 North Clark in 1876. Building construction date and modification scope were not found.

address_historical: South Park Avenue and Thirty-first Street
predecessor_or_rebuild_of: First Baptist Church main building completed in 1875
postfire_code_context: The masonry addition followed the July 1874 fire and complied with the citywide fire-limit environment.
notes: The main church was completed in 1875; the attached Sunday-school portion is reported as completed in 1876. Later alteration and survival of this specific fabric require architectural confirmation.
